### 2026-09-01: `P2-T7` split into three subtasks, `P2-T7a` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 2. `P2-T7` is split into `P2-T7a` through `P2-T7c`. `P2-T7a` is
  complete; `P2-T7b` is next.
- Status at session end: An owner that passes both gates can now hold a reusable Template and author
  the one Version of it that is still editable. A Template identity and that first editable Version
  are created together, because a Template with no editable Version is a name nothing can be said
  about. The Version is then configured as one authored document rather than as independently
  editable settings: the parts of a configuration live in eight tables joined by composite keys, with
  one-way relations and ordering constraints between them, so a partial edit has no coherent reading.
  A section removed while its requirements remain, or a substitute kept after the document it stood
  in for is gone, would render as something no author ever stated. Replacing the whole document means
  what is stored is always exactly one statement. Positions are not authored at all: a section takes
  the position it is listed at and a requirement the position it is listed at within its section, so
  a stored configuration cannot hold a gap, a duplicate, or two orders for one thing. Requirement
  identities are deliberately outside the replaced document, because they belong to the definition
  rather than the version: a rewrite reuses the identity behind a key it still names, creates one for
  a key it names for the first time, and leaves behind the identity of a key it stops naming for a
  later version to ask about again. What a requirement asks for cannot change, since a response
  recorded against it would silently mean something else. Configuration cannot reach a Version that
  has stopped being a draft. Who may author is a role and Share decision about the owner the
  configuration names rather than about whichever organization the caller has selected, a person
  authoring for themselves is the owner or nobody, and every change files under that owner's audit
  ownership rather than under the platform. The platform itself is refused as a Template owner: it is
  storable as one but is neither a paying subject nor a holder of a release grant, so a
  platform-owned Template would reach neither gate and would leave the capability open in exactly the
  deployments it is meant to be closed in.

- Decisions made:
  - `P2-T7` was split three ways. Its five named operations divide cleanly into authoring a draft,
    freezing one, and the lifecycle after a Version has frozen, and the first has to establish the
    authorization, entitlement, audit, and read contracts the other two reuse. Doing all five at once
    would also have meant one session touching eight tables, the authorization stack, the audit
    catalog, and the read contract together.
  - A draft is replaced whole rather than patched. A sparse edit across eight tables with composite
    freeze guards has no coherent partial reading, and the alternative is a large API whose failure
    modes are combinations nobody authored.
  - Positions are derived from the authored order rather than accepted from the author. An author who
    could state a position could state a gap or a duplicate, and both stored uniqueness constraints
    exist precisely to refuse that. Deriving them makes the refusal unreachable instead of handled.
  - Validation is split by what the fact is about. Coherence between parts of one document lives in
    the validator and names the offending key. Contradictions inside one stored row are left to the
    constraints that already refuse them, because restating them would create a second rule to keep
    in step. Cross-cutting configuration validation stays with `P2-T10` as planned.
  - Refusing a requirement from changing what it asks for lives in the writer rather than the
    validator, because it is a fact about the definition's stored identities rather than about the
    document, and the validator is pure by design.
  - The platform is refused as a Template owner. It is storable as one, but it is not a paying
    subject and holds no release grant, so a platform-owned Template would answer to neither gate.
    Given the phase requirement that this capability stay closed by default, an owner that cannot
    hold the gates cannot hold a Template. Storage keeps the scope for a later platform catalog if
    one is ever wanted, which is a separate decision with its own gate to design.
  - The refusal lives in the entitlement guard rather than in the service, so there is one place that
    answers the question for every owner and no path that special-cases an allowance.
  - Template configuration mutations get their own audit category now rather than waiting for
    `P3-T2`. The progress rules refuse to check a task that introduces a mutation without a
    classified audit event, and filing Template configuration under `FIELD_SCHEMA` would have said
    something untrue about what the event is. `P3-T2` extends the same category with the runtime
    request event types; it does not create it.
  - The audit owner is the stored owner and never falls back to platform scope. This is the first
    consumer of the personal audit ownership `P2-T1f` added, and a personally owned Template recorded
    as the platform's would be readable by the wrong audience.
  - Reads answer to both gates as well as writes, so an unreleased capability exposes no
    configuration rather than exposing a read-only view of it.
  - Template configuration capabilities go to organization owners and administrators only, not to
    members. Authoring reusable configuration is a settings activity, and default-deny is the right
    starting point for a capability that is still being built.
  - A list has its own contract with no configuration in it. Reusing the full shape would have meant
    a whole configuration projection per listed Template, and representing "not loaded" as an empty
    section list would have made the contract ambiguous.
  - `InformationRequestTemplateVersionCapabilityRepository` is untouched by this task. It is still
    read only by `InformationRequestTemplateCapabilityGate`, and `P2-T7b` has to settle who writes it
    before the publishing service does.

### 2026-09-01: `P2-T6` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 2. `P2-T6` is complete; `P2-T7` is next.
- Status at session end: A frozen Version now states what it needs a runtime to supply, and that
  statement is separated into the two halves that are answered in different places. Which
  capabilities are needed is a fact about the configuration, so it is derived from what the Version
  actually configures and held in the database: requesting typed data, a document, or an assertion
  each needs the runtime that collects that kind of answer, anything collected at all needs the
  runtime that submits the result, and the optional policies a binding or an evidence policy may
  state each need the runtime that executes them. Publication compares the recorded set against the
  derived one and refuses a disagreement in either direction, because a missing entry would let a
  Version be issued into a runtime that cannot serve it and an extra one would refuse issuance for a
  reason no author could act on. Which contract version of each is needed is recorded rather than
  derived, because whether an installed runtime can serve it is a code fact. That second question is
  asked at issuance rather than at publication: configuration outlives any one deployment, so a
  Version published where everything is installed has to stay publishable where it is not, and
  refusing publication would make a Template unauthorable until the runtime caught up. An installed
  executor serves a range of contract versions, so raising one does not strand what was already
  published against the older contract. No executor is installed, so nothing is served and every
  Version that requires anything is refused at issuance, which is the intended default-off state.
- Tests added first: `InformationRequestTemplateCapabilityContractTest`, seven clean-schema and
  populated-baseline PostgreSQL contract tests covering the recorded row and its closed vocabulary,
  per-Version uniqueness, the contract-version floor, the derivation over an empty Version, over the
  smallest thing a Version can ask for, and over a Version exercising all eleven capabilities, the
  derivation reading one Version rather than its definition, publication refusing an unrecorded and a
  partially recorded set, publication refusing an unconfigured capability, the freeze of the recorded

    unchanged, and the guard still calls the function only on the transition into `PUBLISHED`, so a
    Version published before this migration is not revalidated.
  - `InformationRequestCapability` declares the eleven capabilities and the current contract version
    of each, and `InformationRequestCapabilityRequirement` pairs one with the contract version a
    Version was frozen against. `InformationRequestCapabilityExecutor` is what a deployment installs
    to state that it can serve a capability, over a range of contract versions rather than one.
  - `InstalledCapabilities` indexes the executors and answers what is served, refusing at
    construction a duplicate claim, a range starting below the first contract, an empty range, and an
    executor implementing a contract the platform has not declared. It is a plain class rather than a
    bean, so a test can build an explicit installation without a container.
    `InformationRequestCapabilityExecutorRegistry` is the thin CDI bean that builds one from the
    discovered executors at startup.
  - `InformationRequestTemplateCapabilityGate` reads what a Version recorded and answers whether this
    deployment can serve it, naming every unserved requirement rather than the first through
    `InformationRequestCapabilityNotInstalledException`. This is the check `P3-T10` issuance calls.

  (`auditWorkspaceOverviewArticle.tsx`, `platformAdministrationOverviewArticle.tsx`,
  `trustedOrganizationsAdministrationArticle.tsx`, `workflowOverviewArticle.tsx`) and every match was
  read in full; all of them describe an authorization capability from the `Action` and `Capability`
  stack, which is a different concept from a runtime executor capability, so no statement became
  inaccurate. No update is needed because this task adds no route, endpoint, UI, or user-visible
  behavior.
- Decisions made:
  - The set of capabilities is derived from the configuration rather than authored. An author who
    could name the set could name a shorter one, and the whole point of the record is to be the thing
    issuance trusts. Derivation belongs beside the configuration it reads, which is why it is a SQL
    function called by publication rather than only a service rule.
  - The contract version is not derived, because it is a code fact. Putting the current contract
    version of each capability in a seeded table would create two sources of truth that drift, and a
    migration would be needed to raise one. This follows the choice `SchemaTargetRegistry` already
    made for the schema-target vocabulary: the platform fact lives in code, and the database records
    what a row stated.
  - Publication requires the record; issuance requires the runtime. Refusing publication when the
    runtime is missing would tie authoring to the deployment that happens to be running, and the same
    Template would be publishable on one installation and not another. Refusing issuance instead
    keeps configuration portable and puts the refusal where somebody can act on it.
  - Both directions of the comparison are enforced. A missing entry is the dangerous one, but an
    extra entry is a permanent unexplainable issuance refusal, because a published Version is frozen
    and the entry can never be removed.
  - An executor declares a range of contract versions rather than one. Without the range, raising a
    capability's contract version would immediately strand every Version already published against
    the older one, which is exactly the outcome versioning exists to avoid. An executor claiming a
    contract above the platform's declared one fails startup, because that is a stale executor rather
    than a newer capability.
  - `RESPONSE_SUBMISSION` is derived from the presence of any binding rather than being a constant.
    A Version that configures nothing needs nothing, and making the entry unconditional would record
    a requirement that traces to no configured fact.
  - `InstalledCapabilities` is a plain class and the CDI bean wraps it. This is what lets a test
    build the explicit test-only installation the walking-skeleton rule permits, without a container
    and without any production path that can bypass the check.
  - The word capability already means an atomic authorization permission in this codebase
    (`Capability`, `RoleCapabilities`, `Action`). The plan uses the same word for both, so the new
    types carry the `InformationRequest` prefix and live in their own package. Nothing in the
    authorization stack was touched or renamed.
  - No column carries a database default. Both halves of a recorded row are statements a writer has
    to make, and the table is empty.
- Assumptions: nothing writes the capability table yet. The publishing service that derives and
  records the set is `P2-T7`, and the database rules are written to be the last line of defence under
  it rather than the only rule. The first real executor is registered in `P7-T10`, and review and
  correction executors in `P8-T12`; until then the gate refuses everything, which is what
  `P3-T13` relies on when it exposes drafts without issuance.
- Industry-neutrality audit: every table, column, constraint, trigger, function, entity, enum,
  repository, service, exception, and method name uses generic capability, contract, executor,
  version, and publication vocabulary. The eleven capability names describe reusable collection and
  review behaviors rather than any industry's process, no capability names a document kind, an
  issuing body, a territory, or a decision rule, and no shipped row, default, seeded capability, or
  installed executor exists. Test data is neutral synthetic content only: `process-*` namespaces, a
  `collection-pattern` template key, `collected-data` and `supporting-data` sections,
  `supporting-record`, `alternate-record`, `recorded-note` and `recorded-assertion` requirements, a
  `restricted-set` compartment, a `when-note-applies` rule key, a `per-recorded-item` occurrence
  anchor, and `@process.test` addresses. Two materially different neutral patterns are proven: the
  smallest Version, one plain assertion, needing exactly the two capabilities that collect and submit
  it, and a Version asking for typed data and two documents conditionally, per occurrence, in a
  compartment, reviewed, waivable, with a substitute and supporting evidence, needing all eleven. No
  production path branches on any of those names.
- Known risks or blockers: none blocking `P2-T7`. Five things are worth carrying forward, and the
  fifth is the most important one for that task. `request_template_version_guard` is a
  `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` trigger, so a row inserted directly with `status = 'PUBLISHED'` is
  checked by none of the five publication-completeness rules, including the two added here. This is
  V86 behavior rather than anything new, and
  `InformationRequestTemplatePersistenceContractTest.publishedVersion` relies on it, but it means the
  publishing service must create a draft and transition it. A service that inserted a finished
  published Version in one statement would silently bypass every completeness rule the last three
  migrations added. The other four: first,
  publication now compares four more tables against the recorded set, so the publishing service must
  record the derived capabilities before it flips the status, in the same transaction; recording
  afterwards is refused by the freeze guard. Second, the derivation exists twice in intent, in SQL for
  publication and implicitly in whatever `P2-T7` writes, so that service should read the SQL function
  rather than reimplement the rules, and a clone must recompute the set for the new Version rather
  than copy the old rows, which the composite freeze would refuse anyway. Third, the contract
  versions are all 1 today, so no test exercises a genuine range; the first raise of a contract
  version must add one. Fourth, `InformationRequestTemplateCapabilityGate` reads the repository
  directly because no other Information Request service exists yet; when `P2-T7` adds one, the
  ownership of that repository should be settled so two services do not both write it.
- Exact next task: `P2-T7`, implement draft, publish, clone, retire, and create-new-version services.
  Published versions must be immutable and mappable through dedicated DTO mappers. Publication must
  gather the whole configuration, including every Document evidence policy and the derived capability
  set, before it flips the status, because the database refuses an incomplete freeze and refuses any
  addition afterwards.

### 2026-09-01: `P2-T4` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 2. `P2-T4` is complete; `P2-T5` is next.
- Status at session end: A Template requirement now says what kind of thing it asks for, and a
  Template Version now says under what policy it asks for it. The type is `FIELD`, `DOCUMENT`, or
  `RESPONSE_ATTESTATION` and it lives on the stable requirement, so it is covered by the rule that a
  stable identity is never rewritten. Everything a later Version may legitimately restate lives on
  the binding: the wording used to ask, the help beside it, what the nominated party may do with the
  item, whether an answer is owed and what decides that, which party is nominated, whether a
  reviewer must look at the result, which confidentiality compartment the response falls into, and
  which repeated occurrence it is answered against. The two plural parts of that policy, the answers
  a respondent may give and the documents that support an answer, are their own tables keyed to the
  binding and carrying its Version, so the guard already written for sections and bindings freezes
  them with it. Supporting evidence runs one way only, from a requirement that is not a document to
  a requested document, which makes a cycle unreachable rather than merely detected. Publishing a
  Version that binds a Field requirement now requires the Schema Version it resolves against, which
  closes the question `P2-T3` deferred to the task where requirement types are known.

    as `P2-T3` reasoned. The identity guard was widened rather than a separate trigger added, so
    there is one place that answers what a stable requirement identity consists of.
  - Permitted dispositions and supporting evidence are tables rather than serialized lists. Storage
    can then refuse an unregistered disposition and hold both ends of a support relationship to one
    Version, neither of which a serialized list can do, and it matches the direction the repository
    already took when workflow decisions and blueprint participants were normalized.
  - `NOT_ANSWERED` is in the platform disposition vocabulary but is refused as a permitted answer. It
    is the state every requirement starts in, so allowing a Template to permit it would leave an
    unanswered requirement indistinguishable from a resolved one.

    decision roles are absent by construction rather than refused by a check, so the separation
    between giving an answer and reviewing one cannot be configured away. `P3` remains free to define
    the full request-party vocabulary; this is only the set a Template may nominate to answer.
  - Supporting evidence is one-way by type rather than cycle-checked. A relation whose source set and
    target set are disjoint cannot close, so no traversal is needed at write time and none will be
    needed at issuance.

    earlier would force an author to choose the typed-data contract before adding the first Field
    requirement, which is a product constraint this task has no basis to impose on `P2-T7`.

    that the contradiction of permitting `EXCEPTION_REQUESTED` while declaring review `NOT_REQUIRED`
    has a constructive resolution when `P2-T10` adds that validation.

    writer, so both are empty in any supported deployment, and there is no honest type or prompt to
    invent for a row placed by hand. A populated baseline holding such a row stops the upgrade

  ask the same thing more or less strictly without becoming a different requirement. The policy
  covers how many files are expected and how large they may be individually and in total, how many
  pages they may run to, which content types are accepted, and which of issuer, jurisdiction,
  language, issue date, expiry date, coverage period, certification, and signature have to be stated
  about them. All eight of those draw from one three-value vocabulary, because they are the same
  decision asked about different attributes. The bounds measured against those dates, freshness of
  the issue date, validity remaining past the expiry date, and the span and continuity of the covered
  period, are admitted only while the date they count from is required, so no bound exists that
  nothing can evaluate. Restricting which values an attribute accepts is a set keyed by which
  attribute it restricts rather than a column per attribute. What may be supplied instead of the
  Document is a flat set of alternatives. Waiver and technical conformance are stated rather than
  assumed: a Version says whether the requirement may be resolved without the evidence and what
  reaches that outcome, and whether a technically deficient file is refused outright or left to a
  reviewer. Only a requested Document carries any of this, and a Version that asks for one cannot
  freeze without it.

  populated-baseline PostgreSQL contract tests covering policy ownership by requirement type, one

  substitute set with self-reference, non-Document ends, both chain directions and cross-version

- Decisions made:
  - The policy is one-to-one with a Requirement Binding rather than with the stable requirement.
    Strictness is exactly the kind of thing a later Version may legitimately restate, unlike the kind
    of thing being asked for, which V87 fixed to the identity.
  - The eight attribute requirements share one vocabulary rather than each having its own. They are
    the same decision, asked about different attributes, and eight separate vocabularies would drift.
  - Accepted values are one set keyed by attribute rather than one table per restrictable attribute.
    Making a further attribute restrictable then needs no table and no migration for a new shape.
    `CONTENT_TYPE` is restrictable without being one of the captured attributes, because the type of
    a file is read from the file rather than stated by the party supplying it, so the
    uncaptured-attribute publication rule exempts it.
  - Substitution is flat and refused from both ends rather than cycle-checked. This is the same
    technique V87 used for supporting evidence: make the unwanted shape unreachable instead of
    detectable. A self-reference is left to a check constraint, which is why the test proves it
    before any substitute exists; once one does, the flatness rule refuses it first.
  - Publication now requires a policy for every Document Binding, by direct analogy with the V87
    rule that a Version requesting typed data must name its Schema Version. An absent policy is
    indistinguishable from an author who never reached the question, and publication is the last
    point at which the answer can still be supplied. A genuinely permissive Document says so with a
    policy that restricts nothing, which is a statement rather than a silence.
  - Waiver policy and the permitted `WAIVED` disposition are checked against each other in both
    directions. A waiver rule no permitted answer reaches never takes effect, and a permitted waived
    answer with no rule behind it is an outcome nothing governs.
  - Technical conformance is stated as what happens to a deficient file, not as which checks run.
    Scanning and detected-content inspection are unconditional in Phase 6 and must not be
    configurable; the concrete technical bounds are the accepted content types and the size and page
    limits of the same policy.
  - `request_template_version_guard` now calls completeness only on the transition into `PUBLISHED`.
    Without that narrowing, a rule added later could retroactively invalidate a Version published
    before it existed. The upgrade test asserts exactly this against a populated baseline.
  - `minimum_remaining_validity_days` admits zero, which means the evidence merely has to be
    unexpired. `maximum_issue_age_days` requires at least one, because a zero-day freshness window
    would refuse everything.
  - No column carries a database default. V87 added its policy columns without one, both tables are
    empty, and forcing a writer to state the policy is the point; the neutral closed-by-default value
    lives on the entity instead.
- Assumptions: nothing writes these tables yet. The draft, publish, clone, retire, and new-version
  services are `P2-T7`, and the guards are written to be the last line of defence under those
  services rather than the only rule. Evaluation of the policy against real files is `P6-T5`; this
  task only makes the policy expressible and coherent.
- Industry-neutrality audit: every table, column, constraint, index, trigger, function, entity, enum,
  repository, and method name uses generic evidence, document, file, attribute, coverage, waiver,
  conformance, substitute, and publication vocabulary. No attribute names a particular document kind,
  issuing body, territory, or retention rule, and no shipped row, default, or seeded policy exists.
  Test data is neutral synthetic content only: `process-*` namespaces, a `collection-pattern` template
  key, `collected-data` and `supporting-data` sections, `supporting-record`, `alternate-record`,
  `further-record`, `recorded-note` and `recorded-assertion` requirements, a
  `primary-record-source` issuer, a `region-a` jurisdiction, and `@process.test` addresses. Two
  materially different neutral evidence patterns are proven: a single unrestricted file judged only
  by its presence, and a multi-file collection bounded by count, size, pages, accepted content types,
  a required issuer and jurisdiction, a freshness window, remaining validity, a continuous minimum
  coverage span, review-approved waiver, and reviewable deficiency, with a flat set of alternatives.
  No production path branches on any of those names.
- Known risks or blockers: none blocking `P2-T6`. Three things are worth carrying forward. First,
  publication completeness is a database-level rule over four tables, so a publishing service must
  gather the whole configuration, including every Document policy, before it flips the status;
  publishing first and completing afterwards is refused by design. Second, the accepted-value set
  reaches its policy through a composite foreign key on the Version, so a service that moves a policy
  between Versions cannot exist and a clone must write new rows rather than repoint old ones. Third,
  `ux_request_template_evidence_policy_binding` is an immediate unique constraint, so replacing a
  Document's policy inside one draft means deleting before inserting, which `P2-T7` should do in one
  statement or one ordered transaction.
- Exact next task: `P2-T6`, add a versioned Template capability schema and executor registry.

### 2026-09-01: `P2-T3` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 2. `P2-T3` is complete; `P2-T4` is next.
- Status at session end: Reusable request configuration now persists as five records. A Template
  Definition is the stable identity one owner holds, in the platform, organization, or personal key
  space. A Template Version is one frozen answer to that identity, numbered per definition. A
  Section is an ordered grouping inside one Version, keyed so the same grouping stays recognisable
  across Versions while its position does not. A Requirement is the stable identity of one thing the
  Template asks for, held at the definition so a response recorded against it keeps its meaning. A
  Requirement Binding places one stable requirement into one Version, in one section, at one
  position. Publication freezes a Version and everything it holds; the only later fact recordable
  about it is retirement, and a retired Version stays readable for the requests pinned to it.
  Requirement typing and respondent policy are deliberately absent and are `P2-T4`.
- Tests added first:
  - `InformationRequestTemplateContractTest`, 6 PostgreSQL contracts: the three owner key spaces and
    per-owner key uniqueness; exactly one existing owner per scope kind; per-definition version
    numbering plus the rule that a published or retired Version must say when it became one; a
    binding refused when its section belongs to another Version, when its requirement belongs to
    another definition, when the Version already binds that requirement, and a section refused when
    another already holds its position; per-definition requirement key uniqueness and the refusal of
    any rewrite of a stable requirement identity; and a published Version whose row, sections, and
    bindings all stop changing while retirement still succeeds and removes nothing.
  - `InformationRequestTemplatePersistenceContractTest`, 5 Quarkus PostgreSQL contracts: all five
    records survive the round trip through the mapped entities; a key lookup answers for one owner
    rather than for everybody without an organization; version, section, requirement, and binding
    lookups answer only for their own parent; a Version reads its sections and bindings in the order
    it states rather than in insertion order; and published Versions resolve oldest first with the
    latest published one distinct from a later draft.

    configuration.
  - Section keys and positions are unique per Version. Requirement keys are unique per definition.

    belong to this Version and the requirement to this Version's definition. Because the tenant is a
    property of the definition, that also prevents a Version from holding another owner's
    requirement without adding owner columns to any child table.

    refuses removal, a retired Version accepts nothing, sections and bindings refuse insertion,
    update, and deletion whenever either the old or the new Version is not a draft, and a stable

### 2026-09-01: `P2-T2` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 2. `P2-T2` is complete; `P2-T3` is next.
- Status at session end: A request subject now has a stable opaque identity owned by exactly one
  organization or one person. The identity records only its generic subject kind and ownership,
  while optional external aliases live in a separate tenant-scoped table with the principal and
  time that authorized each alias. Merge and supersession lineage is append-only, cannot cross a
  tenant, cannot fork from one source, and cannot form a cycle. The model remains distinct from the
  serialized `DomainEvent.SubjectRef` event-envelope type.
- Tests added first: `SubjectIdentityRefContractTest` with five PostgreSQL contracts covering
  organization and personal ownership, non-account `ASSET` and `RECORD` subjects, exact owner and
  subject-kind constraints, optional authorized external identifiers, tenant-bound merge and
  supersession, single-successor lineage, cycle refusal, and append-only history.
- Failure observed before implementation:
  - The first sandboxed Maven invocation could not reach Maven resources, so it did not count as
    the behavioral red state.
  - The first escalated invocation exposed a test-fixture compilation error because the nested
    fixture could not call its enclosing helpers. Making the fixture an inner class corrected the
    test without changing production code.
  - The valid pre-implementation run reached PostgreSQL: 5 tests ran, with 1 failure and 4 errors,
    because `subject_identity_ref` did not exist. This was the intended behavioral red state.
- Implementation completed:
  - Added `SubjectIdentityRef`, `SubjectIdentityExternalIdentifier`, and
    `SubjectIdentityTransition` entities plus dedicated owner, subject-kind, and transition enums.
  - Added repositories under the `informationrequest` domain with tenant-qualified identity,
    alias, and source-lineage lookups.
  - V85 creates the three tables. Explicit organization and user foreign keys plus a generated
    owner ID preserve a compact composite tenant key. Composite foreign keys bind every alias and
    both ends of every transition to that exact tenant.
  - External aliases require an authority, identifier type, value, authorizing canonical principal,
    and authorization time. Tenant-local uniqueness prevents one external identity from naming two
    subjects while permitting independent tenants to use the same external vocabulary.
  - A source may have one `MERGED` or `SUPERSEDED` successor. A recursive insertion guard refuses
    cycles, and a database trigger refuses updates or deletion of recorded lineage.

### 2026-09-01: `P2-T1e` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 2. `P2-T1e` is complete; `P2-T1f` is next.
- Status at session end: A capability that is still being built now answers to two independent
  decisions, and holding one without the other is refused. The commercial decision stays where it
  was, a row an App Administrator records against an owner. The new operational decision is
  deployment configuration naming the owners this deployment has turned the capability on for. No
  environment names anybody, so the gate refuses everybody today. `INFORMATION_REQUESTS` is the only
  capability declared under controlled release, and the session contract no longer advertises it to
  an owner who holds the commercial grant alone.
- Shape decision, which the previous handoff left open: the rollout grant is configuration, not
  storage. Three reasons decided it. A commercial grant is a fact about a customer and must travel
  with the data; readiness is a fact about a deployment and must not, or restoring production data
  into a test environment would carry the release state with it. The two are made by different
  people at different times, and one table with two meanings is the collapse the plan forbids. And
  storage would have needed a migration, an administration surface, and audit for a value that an
  operator sets once per environment.
- Second decision, also left open by the previous handoff: the gate refuses the capability, never the
  grant. An App Administrator can still record an `INFORMATION_REQUESTS` commercial grant with no
  rollout grant present. Refusing the grant would make a stored commercial record depend on the
  configuration of whichever environment it was recorded in, and would collapse the two decisions
  into one from the other direction.
- Tests added first:
  - `service/subscription/FeatureRolloutConfigServiceTest.kt`, 8 tests, new file. Nothing configured
    denies every owner and every capability; a grant names one capability, one owner kind, and one
    owner, and is read back for exactly that triple; an organization grant is not read by an
    individual account holding the same id; a grant opens only the capability it names; several
    grants are read independently; casing and surrounding whitespace do not change what an entry
    means; six malformed entries each grant nothing; and an unreadable entry does not withdraw a
    readable one beside it.
  - `service/subscription/FeatureRolloutGateTest.kt`, 14 tests, new file. Neither grant refuses for
    want of the commercial one; the commercial grant alone refuses as `FEATURE_NOT_RELEASED`; the
    rollout grant alone refuses as `FEATURE_NOT_INCLUDED`; both grants held by the same owner reach
    the capability; a grant made for one owner does not reach another; report-only and disabled
    enforcement each still refuse both one-sided cases while a released capability still passes;
    a released capability is unaffected by the rollout configuration; the availability read answers
    the same two grants without refusing; the capability declares itself under controlled release;
    the resolved commercial position still reports the entitlement on its own; and the session
    contract reports the capability only once both grants exist while still reporting every released
    capability.
  - `service/subscription/ProductionSubscriptionEnforcementConfigurationTest.kt`, 1 test added to an
    existing file. The shipped default names nobody and no environment file ships a grant.
  - `service/subscription/PlanCatalogTest.kt` now derives its held-back set from the capability
    declaration instead of restating it, and asserts that set is exactly `INFORMATION_REQUESTS`, so
    the two statements cannot drift apart.
- Failure observed before implementation:
  - The three new production shapes were added carrying no behaviour, because a compilation error is
    not the required red. That run: 53 tests, 13 failures, 0 errors.
  - `FeatureRolloutConfigServiceTest`: 5 failures, each `expected: <true> but was: <false>`, the
    parser answering nothing for a grant that was configured.
  - `FeatureRolloutGateTest`: 6 failures. `Expected SubscriptionDenialException to be thrown, but
    nothing was thrown` for report-only, disabled enforcement, and the commercial grant alone;
    `expected: <true> but was: <false>` for the capability declaring itself under controlled release;
    and the availability read and the one-owner-does-not-reach-another case both answering as though
    only the commercial decision existed.
  - `PlanCatalogTest`: 2 failures. With no capability declaring itself under controlled release the
    derived held-back set was empty, so `expected: <[INFORMATION_REQUESTS]> but was: <[]>` and the
    Business plan assertion, which is stated as every feature minus that set, failed with it.
  - A later run added the session-contract test on its own: 17 tests, 1 failure, `A commercial grant
    alone must not advertise a capability the owner cannot reach ==> expected: <false> but was:
    <true>`.
- Implementation completed:
  - `FeatureRolloutConfigService` in `service/subscription/` reads `app.subscription.rollout.grants`
    and answers `isGranted(owner, feature)` and `grantedFeatures(owner)`. An entry is
    `FEATURE:OWNER_TYPE:OWNER_ID`, entries are comma separated, and the parsed form is keyed by
    `SubscriptionContext` so an organization and an individual account with the same id never read
    each other's grants. An entry that cannot be read is logged and ignored rather than widened, so
    a typo leaves the capability closed.
  - `PlanFeature` gained `requiresRolloutGrant`, and `INFORMATION_REQUESTS` sets it. Whether a
    capability is finished is a fact about the code, so it is declared in the code and no operator
    can switch the requirement off; only the per-owner grant is configurable.
  - `SubscriptionAccessService.requireFeature` branches to `requireReleasedFeature` for a capability
    under controlled release, which applies both decisions and refuses through `refuse`, a new
    private method that always records and raises. The commercial half is checked first so an owner
    who holds neither is told the commercially meaningful thing rather than being told about a
    release they were never entitled to.
  - Neither half observes `SubscriptionEnforcementMode`. That mode exists so an environment can watch
    what commercial policy would refuse before customers are blocked, and an unfinished capability
    must not become reachable by relaxing an unrelated commercial setting. Without this,
    `REPORT_ONLY` would have let the rollout grant alone through and broken the exit criterion.
  - `apply` now delegates its enforcing branch to `refuse` rather than keeping a second copy of the
    log line and the throw.
  - `SubscriptionDenialReason.FEATURE_NOT_RELEASED` and `SubscriptionDenialFactory.featureNotReleased`
    produce the refusal. It carries no upgrade hint, because no plan change would help: what is
    missing is readiness, not entitlement. `denialType` maps it to `ROLLOUT` so an operator can tell
    a release refusal from a commercial one in the logs without reading the reason.
  - `SubscriptionAccessService.isFeatureAvailable` and `availableFeatures` are the read side the
    three personal doors will consult. `resolve` deliberately still reports the entitlement, because
    it is documented as the commercial position and the two refusal reasons would collapse into one
    if it did not.
  - `SessionSubscriptionService` reports `availableFeatures` rather than the resolved set, and
    `SubscriptionDtoMapper.toDto` takes them as a parameter defaulting to the resolved set. The
    client decides what to offer from that list, so a list naming something every call site refuses
    would be a promise the product cannot keep.
  - `app.subscription.rollout.grants` is in `application.properties` with the environment override
    and an empty default, documented in place.

- Decisions made:
  - The rollout grant is configuration rather than storage, and the gate refuses the capability
    rather than the grant. Both are recorded above with their reasoning, because the previous handoff
    asked for both to be decided here.
  - Whether a capability is under controlled release is declared on `PlanFeature`, not configured.
    If it were configuration an operator could remove the gate entirely and reach an unfinished
    capability with the commercial grant alone, which is the outcome the gate exists to prevent.
  - The enforcement mode does not soften either half. Stated as its own decision because it is the
    one place this gate deliberately behaves unlike every other commercial check in the service.
  - The commercial half is checked before the release half, which also keeps the released assertion
    in `SubscriptionAccessServiceTest` that an owner holding neither is told the feature is not
    included.
  - `resolve` still reports a granted capability under controlled release, and the narrowing happens
    in `availableFeatures`. `resolve` is documented as the commercial position, and narrowing it
    would make `requireReleasedFeature` unable to tell the two refusals apart.

    frontend chooses what to offer from `EffectiveSubscriptionDto.features`, so leaving it wide would

    individual plan sells, and it used `INFORMATION_REQUESTS`. It now uses `WORKFLOW_AUTOMATION`,

    `FeatureRolloutGateTest`.

    again, so the two cannot drift.

- Industry-neutrality audit: the added production identifiers are `FeatureRolloutConfigService` with
  `isGranted`, `grantedFeatures`, and the private `OwnerFeatureGrant`; the configuration key
  `app.subscription.rollout.grants` and its environment variable `APP_SUBSCRIPTION_ROLLOUT_GRANTS`;
  `PlanFeature.requiresRolloutGrant`; `SubscriptionDenialReason.FEATURE_NOT_RELEASED`;
  `SubscriptionDenialFactory.featureNotReleased`; `SubscriptionAccessService.isFeatureAvailable`,
  `availableFeatures`, `isReleasedTo`, `requireReleasedFeature`, and `refuse`; the log denial type
  `ROLLOUT` and the log event `feature_rollout_configured`; and the
  `SubscriptionDtoMapper.toDto` parameter `availableFeatures`. All are release, commercial, and
  ownership vocabulary naming no industry, customer, or process domain. No production branch reads a
  customer-controlled name: the parser matches a configured string against the platform's own
  `PlanFeature` and `SubscriptionOwnerType` codes and discards anything it does not recognize, and
  the gate compares owner kinds and a boolean the code declares. Nothing branches on a particular
  feature code; `INFORMATION_REQUESTS` is reached only through the generic `requiresRolloutGrant`
  flag, so a second capability under controlled release would need no new code. Test data is neutral:
  fixed synthetic UUIDs, the platform's own feature codes, and `NOT_A_FEATURE` and
  `NOT_AN_OWNER_KIND` for the entries that must be refused. The capability was validated against two
  materially different neutral owner patterns through one code path: an organization and an
  individual account, each granted separately, each proven not to inherit the other's grant when
  their ids are equal, and each refused identically when either half of its pair is missing. It was
  also validated against two materially different capability patterns: one under controlled release,
  which is refused on both halves in every enforcement mode, and one released, whose behaviour is
  unchanged in every one of those modes.
- Known risks or blockers: none blocking `P2-T1f`.
  - Closed since the last session: an `INFORMATION_REQUESTS` commercial grant was the only decision
    standing between an owner and an unfinished capability, with no separate statement that a
    deployment was ready to serve it; and the session contract would have advertised such a
    capability to the client on that grant alone.
  - New: a rollout grant is per-deployment configuration, so it does not travel with a database
    restore and does not appear in any audit record. That is the intended trade and the reason
    configuration was chosen, but it means the answer to "who was this turned on for" lives in
    deployment configuration and its change history, not in Platform Audit. The service logs
    `event=feature_rollout_configured` with the number of owners and grants read at startup so a
    deployment can be seen to be configured at all.
  - New: an unreadable grant entry is ignored with a warning rather than failing startup. It fails
    closed, but an operator who mistypes an id will see the capability stay shut rather than a hard
    failure, and must read the warning to find out why.
  - New: the two grants can now disagree in a way an App Administrator cannot see. The platform-admin
    editor shows the commercial grant and says nothing about release readiness, so an administrator
    can grant `INFORMATION_REQUESTS` and be unable to tell from any screen why it does nothing. That

  override table records an organization or a person, admits exactly one owner per row, keys
  uniqueness per owner, and carries every released organization row across untouched. Resolution
  reads the decisions of the owner being resolved, so an individual account can now be granted a
  feature its plan omits or have one withdrawn, which the organization path could already do and the
  individual path silently could not. `INFORMATION_REQUESTS` exists as a plan feature that no plan

  records a personal grant. Storage plus resolution is one bounded behaviour with its own red set;
  the writer is another. Shipping only the first would leave a table whose personal half nothing
  writes, which is the second of the three failure modes this plan's baseline section warns about,
  so the writer is named as `P2-T1d2` rather than left implied.

- Implementation completed:
  - `V83__subscription_feature_entitlement_owner.sql` renames `organization_feature_entitlement` to
    `subscription_feature_entitlement` with its primary key, both foreign keys, the code check, and
    the organization index, adds `owner_type` and `app_user_id`, sets every existing row to the
    organization owner it always had, makes `organization_id` nullable, and adds the owner check that
    admits exactly one owner per kind. The released `UNIQUE (organization_id, feature_code)` is
    dropped for a unique index on `(owner_type, COALESCE(organization_id, app_user_id),
    feature_code)`: once the organization id is nullable that constraint stops constraining a
    personal row, because two of a person's rows would both hold NULL there and neither would be
    refused. The owner kind leads the expression so an organization and a person with equal ids keep
    separate key spaces, and the owner check guarantees exactly one of the two columns contributes,
    so no sentinel is needed.
  - There is one owner check rather than a separate vocabulary check. PostgreSQL evaluates CHECK
    constraints in name order, so a separate `..._owner_type` check would sort after `..._owner` and
    never be the one reported; the single check already admits exactly the two owner kinds and
    nothing else, which is what the constraint name says.
  - `SubscriptionFeatureEntitlement` replaces `OrganizationFeatureEntitlement`, and
    `SubscriptionFeatureEntitlementRepository` in `repository/subscription/` replaces the one in
    `repository/organization/`, gaining `findByAppUserId`. Each lookup names the owner column that
    belongs to its owner kind rather than matching an id against both. The owner kind is a string on
    the entity, matching the plan and status codes the neighbouring subscription policy entities
    already store as strings, rather than importing a service enum into the entity layer.
  - `SubscriptionPolicyService.organizationFeatureOverrides(organizationId)` became
    `featureOverrides(context)`, which reads the decisions of whichever owner the context names.
    `EffectiveSubscriptionFactory.fromUserPolicy` takes the overrides and applies them through the
    same `applyOverrides` the organization path already used, and `SubscriptionAccessService`
    resolves them for a user the same way it always did for an organization.
  - `fromUserPolicy` takes the overrides as a required parameter rather than defaulting to none. A
    default would let a future caller resolve an individual without their decisions and never notice,
    which is exactly the bug being removed here. Eight test call sites now state that they pass none.

### 2026-08-31: `P2-T1c` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 2. `P2-T1c` is complete; `P2-T1d` is next.
- Status at session end: A Schema now says which kind of resource it was written for, and the
  platform reads that answer instead of assuming it. `INFORMATION_REQUEST` is a declared target
  beside `EXCHANGE`, an author states the target and an undeclared one is refused, a configured
  default is checked against the target the caller is configuring rather than against a literal, and
  an adapter may only govern a resource some Schema can be written for. No migration: the column that
  stores the answer constrains nothing, and a test now holds that down rather than assuming it.

    one is refused and the refusal names it; a caller naming no target still means the Exchange it
    always meant; a named target is read as a code rather than as the caller typed it; an adapter may
    only govern a resource some Schema can be written for; two adapters may not claim one resource;

- Implementation completed:
  - `SchemaTargetRegistry` declares the resource types a Schema may be written for and is the only
    place that names them. It answers the default target for a caller that names none, normalizes and
    validates a requested one, and fails an undeclared one closed. The Exchange code is taken from
    `ResourceType.EXCHANGE`, so the two stay tied; `INFORMATION_REQUEST` is a declared constant
    because the authorization stack has no resource type for it yet.
  - `SchemaDefinitionService.createSchema` resolves the requested target through the registry and
    writes what it resolved. It no longer writes `"EXCHANGE"` as a literal, and a request naming a
    target nobody declared is refused before anything is saved.
  - `SchemaDefinitionService.validateDefaultsForSchema` takes the resource type the caller is
    configuring defaults for, validates it against the registry, and compares the Schema's target to
    that instead of to `ResourceType.EXCHANGE.name`. `BlueprintDefinitionService` passes the Exchange,
    which is a true statement where it now sits: a blueprint's defaults are the values the Exchange it
    creates starts with. Moving it there removed the Fields engine's assumption without moving the
    assumption anywhere else.
  - `SchemaDefinition.targetResourceType` became `lateinit`. The entity no longer supplies a target,
    because defaulting to any one kind silently mislabels every other kind, and silently mislabelling
    is exactly the failure this task removes. The database keeps its own `DEFAULT 'EXCHANGE'`, which
    is what a row inserted outside the application still means.
  - `FieldResourceAdapterRegistry` indexing moved into `indexAdapters`, which now also refuses an
    adapter governing a resource type no Schema may be written for. Such an adapter could never be
    given a Schema, because an assignment requires one written for exactly that type, so it is a
    startup failure rather than a dormant misconfiguration. Extracting the function is what makes the
    rule testable; the CDI class keeps its field injection.
  - `ExchangeFieldsTab` offers only Schemas written for an Exchange. The Exchange creation wizard, the
    blueprint field-defaults tab, and the workflow applicability editor already filtered on the
    target; this picker did not, and once a second target exists it would have offered a Schema the
    server then refuses.

- Decisions made:
  - The declared targets and the installed adapters are two separate statements. Declaring a target
    says a Schema may name it; installing an adapter says a resource of that type can carry one.
    Keeping them apart is what lets `INFORMATION_REQUEST` be a target now, before the resource that
    will hold one exists, without inventing a stub adapter for a table that is not there. The
    relationship is enforced in one direction only: every adapter must govern a declared target,
    because an adapter for a type no Schema can name could never be given a Schema.
  - The registry is a set of codes rather than a per-target capability object. Every rule this task
    needs, membership, the default, and the two comparisons, reads the code alone. A per-target flag
    with no rule behind it would be speculation, and the shape can grow when a rule actually differs.
  - `validateDefaultsForSchema` takes the target from its caller rather than reading a capability off
    the Schema. The rule being enforced is the caller's, not the Schema's: what makes an Exchange
    blueprint's defaults valid is that they are going onto an Exchange. Encoding it as a Schema
    property would have restated the same literal one level down.

    helper had been relying on the default and now says what it means.
  - `INFORMATION_REQUEST` is a plain constant rather than a `ResourceType` entry. Adding it to
    `ResourceType` would claim the authorization and resource-context registries know the resource,
    which they do not; that claim belongs to `P3-T1`, which adds the resource for real.
  - A Schema written for an information request can be created and published now, by an
    organization administrator calling the API directly. It cannot be assigned to anything, because
    no adapter governs that resource type, and no screen offers the target. It is inert
    configuration, and gating its creation is the rollout gate's job, not the target registry's.

  capability name, a request for information, and is not read as a customer label anywhere. No

  Definition, a Schema Definition, and the assignment of one each carry `scope_user_id`, each scope
  kind admits exactly one owner, and each owner has its own key space. Nothing resolves a personal

  subtasks: `P2-T1a` ownership storage, `P2-T1b` personal-scope code reachability, `P2-T1c` the

  migration with no UI impact, and the closed door is unreachable from any screen.
- Decisions made:
  - The unique indexes fold both owner columns into one `COALESCE(scope_org_id, scope_user_id,
    sentinel)` expression rather than adding `scope_user_id` as a fourth index column. The owner check
    guarantees at most one of the two is set, so the expression is unambiguous, and keeping the scope
    kind in front means an organization id and a user id that happen to be equal still occupy
    different key spaces. A fourth column would have made the platform sentinel row and a personal row
    differ only by which column held the sentinel, which is harder to reason about, not easier.
  - The two owner checks were renamed from `ck_..._scope_org` to `ck_..._scope_owner`. They no longer
    constrain the organization column alone, and a constraint name that appears in a refusal message
    should say what it enforces.
  - The assignment owner check is added after a repair rather than as `NOT VALID`. An assignment's
    scope is a copy of its definition's, so the definition is an authority the repair can use, and
    leaving rows unvalidated would mean the invariant is documented but not held.
  - The personal owner parameter on `findByKey` is required rather than defaulted to null. A default
    would have let both call sites keep the cross-person behaviour without anybody noticing, which is
    the exact bug the parameter exists to prevent.
  - `PERSONAL` is refused at `resolveCreateScope` rather than left to fail deeper. Extending the enum
    made a request naming the personal scope an accepted input on both create endpoints the same day;
    without the refusal the caller would have received an internal error from a `requireNotNull` on a
    missing organization, or a constraint violation, depending on whether subscription enforcement was
    evaluating. Closing it is part of extending the enum, not separate work.
  - The two `requireScopeAccess` sites take an explicit `PERSONAL -> Unit` branch that falls through
    to the existing denial, not an `else`. Failing closed is right for now, and keeping the `when`
    exhaustive is what made the compiler point at both sites in the first place.
- Assumptions: none new.
- Industry-neutrality audit: the added identifiers are `scope_user_id`, `ck_field_def_scope_owner`,
  `ck_schema_def_scope_owner`, `ck_assignment_scope_owner`, `ix_field_def_user`, `ix_schema_def_user`,
  `FieldScopeKind.PERSONAL`, `scopeUserId`, and three test classes named for personal ownership and
  scope. All are ownership and scope vocabulary naming no industry, customer, or process domain. No
  production branch reads a customer-controlled name; the new branches read the scope kind only. Test
  data is the neutral process vocabulary the Phase 1 fixtures already use: a `process` namespace,
  `recorded-note` and `process-data` keys, a Process Owner Org, and `@process.test` owners. The
  capability was validated against two materially different neutral patterns: two different people
  holding the same key, and one key held by the platform, an organization, and a person at the same
  time, including the case where the person's id is the sentinel the released index folded onto.

  they cannot disagree. The Details form no longer asks the schema-configuration surface what the

- Decisions made:
  - The descriptions ride on the assignment projection rather than on a second Exchange-scoped
    endpoint. A separate endpoint would have to resolve the same assignment, build the same gate, and
    narrow the same version, and any drift between the two answers would be a disclosure. One
    response also means a consumer cannot render a form from one version of the truth and save
    against another.
  - The mapper takes the resolved questions rather than two finished lists. Passing both lists would
    have left the invariant to a convention at every call site; deriving both from one list makes a
    projection that describes what it withholds unrepresentable.
  - The envelope is still returned to a caller shown nothing, with both lists empty. That a Schema
    governs the Exchange is not what the audience rule withholds, the empty `fields` list already
    conveyed exactly this, and a consumer needs the difference between nothing shared and nothing
    assigned to say something true to the reader.
  - A binding is described to a caller only if its answer is projected to them, which is the READ
    decision, not the WRITE one. A read-only binding is therefore described and rendered as
    uneditable, exactly as before, and the client's sparse payload keeps excluding it.
  - The nothing-shared message stopped being conditional on the Exchange being read-only rather than
    gaining a second wording for drafts. Publishing requires at least one binding, so the only caller
    who reaches the message is one whose questions were withheld, or one whose schema records cannot
    be loaded at all, and what it says is true of the first and not misleading for the second.
  - `FieldValuesReadOnly` lost its value-only fallback rather than keeping it as insurance. It is now
    unreachable, and what it did was invent a binding per value with a fabricated classification, so
    keeping it would have preserved a second and weaker answer to the question this task exists to
    give one answer to.
  - The scope-authorized resolved-schema view stays, and stays scope-authorized. Exchange creation
    and the Workflow applicability editor still read it, and both are configuration surfaces used
    before any assignment exists, so there is no projection for them to read instead.

  - The gathering and the shaping are separated rather than moved together into one mapper. The
    reason the mapping was hard to test was not where it lived but that it read from repositories
    while it built. Splitting on that line is what makes the mappers exercisable as records in and a
    response out, and it is also what let both services stop duplicating the same walk.
  - The loader narrows through a plain predicate on the binding rather than taking the binding gate.
    The value path filters by policy and the schema-configuration path does not, and a loader that
    took the gate would force the configuration surface to invent one. The predicate keeps the loader
    ignorant of who is asking, which is the property `P1-T8b` needs when it makes one projection
    serve both.

    projection asked for selection rows for every stored answer. Nothing downstream could see them
    for a non-select type, and the write path already treats this as an invariant in
    `recordsSameState`, so this removes a query per stored answer and cannot change a response. A
    test holds it.

    request bodies. It is the shape of an entry in `FieldValueWriteCommand`, so a caller that never
    speaks HTTP still needs it, and `RequestsResponses.kt` already imports it from there. Moving it
    would have made the service layer depend on the resource layer to describe its own command.

    passed a finished tag. `FieldValueSetETag` is pure, and keeping the derivation with the rest of
    the envelope means there is one place that decides what a projection with no set carries.

    task's scope names `SchemaAssignmentService` and the projection DTOs, and those two build the

### 2026-08-31: `P1-T7d` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 1. `P1-T7d` is complete, which completes `P1-T7`; `P1-T8` is next.
  The reusable value-foundation milestone remains in progress.
- Status at session end: The Details form now saves through the canonical surface and states which
  version of the values it is changing. It sends back the validator it was served with the values,
  and it adopts the validator each successful save answers with, so a responder who saves twice in a
  row is not refused for a version that is only still in flight. A save refused because the values
  moved on stores nothing and is not retried: the stored values are read again and the responder is
  told their save was not applied. Their own entries survive that reload, and a field they never
  touched follows the server, so they can see what is now recorded, check it against what they
  typed, and save on top of it. Nothing in the first-party client reaches the superseded write
  surface any more, and the unconditioned save is gone from the service module so nothing can reach
  for it by accident. The help article gains the refusal in the responder's own terms, which is what
  the previous session left owing to this one. The frontend suite, the type check, the build, and
  lint on the changed files pass.

  - `web-app/src/app/exchanges/components/exchange-fields-tab/fieldEditorState.test.ts`, 5 tests:
    every binding of a schema gets a starting value and an unanswered one starts empty; a binding
    stored as empty also starts from nothing rather than from its empty reading; a binding the

- Decisions made:
  - The validator the form states is held in the save hook rather than read straight from the prop on
    each save. A successful save answers with the version it produced, and adopting that immediately
    is what lets a responder save twice in a row: the reload that would otherwise supply it is in
    flight, and waiting for it would refuse the second save for a version that is not actually stale.
    A newly served validator still wins, because the server has then said something more recent than
    the form knows.
  - A read that served no validator makes the save state the wildcard rather than state nothing.
    Stating nothing is refused by the canonical surface, and there is no reload that would produce a
    validator, so a resource holding no set of values would become permanently unsavable. The
    wildcard is also the truth about what such a save read: there is no version to be stale about.
  - The stale answer is a resolved outcome, not a thrown error. It is one of the two answers a
    conditional save is designed to give and the caller has to act on it, so making the caller catch
    and re-classify an exception would put the classification in the wrong place. Every other refusal
    still throws, unchanged, including the demand for a version, which a first-party client that
    always states one can only get if it is broken.
  - The stale classification requires both the status and the machine code. A precondition refused
    for any other reason must not be mistaken for one a reload fixes, and the code is what the server
    added for exactly this.
  - `setExchangeFieldValues` was removed rather than deprecated in place. Leaving an unconditioned
    save on the module invites a future caller into the surface this task exists to stop using, and
    would keep adding to the deprecation measurement the compatibility window is being judged on. A
    test now holds the module to having no such export.
  - The responder's entries are held separately from the stored values instead of the editor state
    being seeded once at mount. Reloading is half of the recovery, and a form that cannot take a
    fresh reading without discarding what the responder typed can only offer one of the two.
    Splitting them lets a field they never touched follow the server while a field they are working
    on keeps their entry.
  - The tab reads the values again without raising its spinner when the form asks. The spinner
    replaces the form, which would destroy both the entries and the message explaining why the save
    was not applied, so the recovery would silently look like a save that did nothing.
  - The form asks for a reload through one callback for both outcomes rather than two. In both cases
    the stored values are no longer what the form was showing, which is the only thing the tab needs
    to know; naming it after the reason would create a distinction the tab does not act on.
  - The save message reads the `errorMessage` the server actually sends. The previous handler looked
    for an `error` property that no response carries, so a validation refusal always showed the
    generic fallback. The stale message has to reach the responder, and so does the reason a value
    was refused.
  - The message tells the responder their save was not applied and that their entries are still
    theirs to check, rather than offering a retry control. A control that resaves is the overwrite
    the condition exists to prevent unless the responder has looked, and the next press of the
    existing Save action is that same save with the current version behind it.

### 2026-08-31: `P1-T7c` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 1. `P1-T7c` is complete; `P1-T7d` is next. The reusable

- Status at session end: An Exchange's answers now have a canonical way to be changed, and it will
  not accept a change from a caller that has not said which version of the answers it read. A caller
  that says nothing is told to start saying it, a caller whose version has been overtaken is told to
  read again and handed the version that is now current, and neither one stores anything. The older
  way in still works exactly as it did for a client that says nothing, but it enforces a version the
  moment one is supplied, it tells its caller in the response that it has been superseded and where
  the replacement lives, and every call through it is recorded so the decision to start demanding a
  version, or to withdraw it, is a measurement rather than a guess. The one place that reads the
  header now understands every shape a caller may legitimately send it: one version, a list of
  versions, a version marked as weak, or the wildcard that names whichever version is current. The
  cross-origin policy of all four profiles was missing both halves of this exchange, so no browser
  client could have sent a version or read one back; both are now allowed and held in place by a
  configuration test. Focused tests, the Fields, Schema and Exchange regression set, the full backend
  suite, and the `web-app` type check pass.

- Decisions made:
  - The header is normalized in one dedicated place at the HTTP edge rather than in the engine or
    inside a resource method. `If-Match` is an HTTP spelling of one engine idea, and the engine
    already has that idea; giving the spelling its own object keeps the second Fields surface, and the
    later no-auth one, from each inventing their own reading of a list or a wildcard.
  - The two surface rules are two named entry points, `required` and `optional`, rather than one
    entry point and a flag. Which status a missing header produces is then a property of the surface
    that called it, visible at the call site, and no flag has to be threaded through the command.
  - `ExpectedRevision` widened from one validator to a set instead of gaining a sibling state. A list
    is a legitimate `If-Match`, satisfied when any listed validator is current, and that is the same
    idea as naming one, not a different one.
  - Validators are compared verbatim, which is what makes a validator marked weak refuse. A weak
    validator names a version that may differ in ways the tag does not capture, and a conditional
    write requires the strong comparison; carrying the `W/` prefix through unchanged gets that for
    free and keeps the validator format known only to the formatter.
  - The wildcard maps onto the unconditioned state rather than onto a case of its own. It states a
    condition, which is what the canonical surface requires, and the condition it states excludes no
    version. `isStated` is what separates it from a missing header, so the measurement is not fooled.
  - A header that carries no validator at all counts as stating nothing, so the canonical surface asks
    for one and the superseded surface keeps its last-write behavior. The alternative, treating a
    malformed header as satisfied, would let a broken client through the exact check the surface
    exists to make.
  - Usage is recorded as a structured log event under one stable name, not as a counter table or a new
    metrics dependency. The service log already reaches CloudWatch Logs, so the window can be measured
    with no migration, no new service, and no new writer on the save path. Every call is recorded
    rather than only the unconditioned ones, because the decision `P12-T1` has to make needs both the
    count that must reach zero and the total it is a share of.
  - The deprecation metadata is `Deprecation: true` plus a `Link` naming the same resource as the
    successor, and deliberately no `Sunset`. A withdrawal date does not exist yet, and emitting one
    would publish a commitment nobody has made; the plan puts that decision after the measurement.
  - The metadata is attached to every response the superseded surface produces, including a refusal,
    because it describes the surface rather than the outcome of one call.
  - The successor link names the identifier the request resolved to rather than the path segment the
    caller sent, so a malformed identifier is answered with the deprecation marker and no link instead
    of having its own text handed back inside a response header.
  - The call is recorded after the caller is resolved and before the save is attempted, so a call
    refused for a stale version still counts as usage of the surface while an unauthenticated or
    malformed one does not.
  - The superseded method kept its name and took the header as an explicit parameter with no default,
    so no call site can silently omit it and quietly test the unconditioned path by accident.
  - The cross-origin change was made here rather than left to the frontend task. Without it the
    canonical surface cannot be called by a browser at all and the validator it returns cannot be
    read, so `P1-T7d` would have started by discovering that the surface it was migrating to was
    unreachable. All four profiles were changed together and a configuration test now holds each one
    to both halves plus the verb, which is the failure mode a single-profile edit would have created.

  notes and as the answers of a first and a second caller. The capability was exercised against two

### 2026-08-31: `P1-T7b` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 1. `P1-T7b` is complete; `P1-T7c` is next. The reusable
  value-foundation milestone remains in progress.
- Status at session end: Every Fields operation now arrives as a command that states four things the
  engine used to work out for itself: which resource it addresses, which set of answers within it,
  who is asking, and which state of that data the caller believes it is changing. The engine reads no
  request state of its own, so the same service can be reached by a registered caller and, later, by
  a recipient-bound one without either door reaching into the other. What a caller may do with one
  question is now asked of the resource that owns it through a single policy, consulted by both the
  projection and the save. A save resolves its set under a write lock, checks the caller's stated
  state against it, and only then stores, so two saves arriving together run one after the other and
  the second is judged against what the first committed. The two ways a precondition can fail carry
  separate machine codes. Focused tests, the full backend suite, and the `web-app` type check pass.
- Tests added first:
  - `src/test/kotlin/.../service/fields/FieldsCommandContractTest.kt`, 7 tests: a save recording the
    caller its own command names rather than any the engine resolved; two callers reaching one engine
    each recorded as themselves; a read authorized as the caller its command names; a save addressed
    to a repetition landing in that repetition and leaving the resource's own answers alone; that save
    advancing only the repetition's count and returning the repetition's validator; a read addressed
