- Decisions made:
  - Every Fields operation has exactly one door, and the door takes a command. The alternative was to
    add command-shaped methods beside the existing ones, which would have left the engine with a
    second entrance that reads the current request for itself, and Phase 4 would have had to remove it
    anyway. The cost was migrating 84 call sites across nine test files; the fixtures absorbed most of
    it, and the tests read better for naming what they do rather than repeating the resource each time.
  - The per-binding policy is a dedicated port reached through the adapter, rather than a second CDI
    registry that would duplicate the discovery and fail-fast code that already exists for adapters.
    One lookup still answers both questions, and a resource domain implements two small interfaces
    instead of one large one.
  - The audience rule moved from the adapter into the Exchange policy, because who counts as an
    outside caller is a per-binding decision and nothing else asked the adapter for it. That also
    keeps the policy free of a back-reference to the adapter, which would have made the two beans
    depend on each other.
  - The rules every resource shares live in `AudienceFieldBindingPolicy`, so a new resource type does
    not restate classification and read-only handling to get them. The Exchange adds nothing to those
    rules, which is what makes it the compatibility implementation the plan asked for.
  - Which lifecycle states allow editing at all stays on the adapter rather than moving into the
    policy. It is one answer for the whole resource, not one per question, and keeping it separate is
    what lets the Information Request adapter answer it differently without touching per-binding
    rules.
  - Only the two denial reasons that have a producer today exist. A denial for scope, response mode,
    or confidentiality is a new reason added when the resource that needs it arrives; the shape
    already carries it.
  - A write refused for audience is refused with the same words as a write naming a binding of
    another schema, so a refusal never tells a caller that a question they cannot see exists.
  - The stated state is carried as the strong validator itself rather than as a parsed identity and
    count. The formatter stays the only thing that knows the format, comparison is one equality, and
    the header parsing that produces it has a caller only in `P1-T7c`.
  - The three precondition states enforce themselves rather than being unpacked by a `when` in the
    service. Adding a state cannot then leave a call site silently accepting it.
  - The Schema assignment validator is derived from the assignment's identity alone and no migration
    was added. An assignment row is written once and never rewritten: choosing a Schema creates it and
    removing the Schema deletes it, so its identity already separates one state from the next, and a
    caller naming the assignment it read cannot spend that claim against the assignment which replaced
    it. A count column with no writer would have burned a migration version on a value that could
    never move. The first operation that rewrites an assignment adds the count behind the same
    formatter, which is why callers never see the format.
  - The Value Set reference was made real rather than decorative. A command naming a repetition reads
    and writes that repetition, and only that repetition's count advances. Nothing creates a
    repetition, so only tests reach the path until Phase 5 owns creation; refusing to create one on
    demand is deliberate, because a repetition exists only where something added it.
  - The save takes a row-level write lock through the repository rather than adopting a JPA `@Version`
    on the set. `@Version` would take ownership of the count away from the service, which counts saves
    rather than row writes, and the lock is what the precondition actually needs: the state it is
    judged against has to be the state the write holds.
  - Both lookups exist in a plain and a locking form rather than a boolean parameter, so a call site
    says which one it wants and a reader can see it without following the argument.
  - Choosing and removing a Schema became one annotated entry point. The four-argument overload that
    worked only because its single caller ran inside `ExchangeInitiationService.initiateExchange` is
    gone, which is the implicit dependency `P3-T6` warned about; the creation path now joins that
    transaction explicitly rather than relying on the absence of an annotation.
  - The `412` and `428` mapping was added in this task rather than deferred, because a machine code
    that cannot reach a client is not something a client can tell apart. The endpoints still state no
    precondition, so nothing can produce either answer through HTTP yet; `P1-T7c` adds the surfaces
    that do.

### 2026-08-31: `P1-T7a` implemented, `P1-T7` split into four subtasks

- Current phase and task: Phase 1. `P1-T7` was split into `P1-T7a` through `P1-T7d` before any code
  was written, because one session cannot carry the command contract, the authorization port, the
  two HTTP surfaces, and the frontend migration together. `P1-T7a` is complete; `P1-T7b` is next.
- Status at session end: A set of answers now counts the changes it has been through, and that count
  is the only thing the entity tag is derived from. The count starts at one, moves by exactly one for
  each save that stores something regardless of how many questions that save answered, stays put for
  a save that stores nothing, and the database refuses any update that would move it backwards. The
  Fields read and every successful Fields mutation return that tag, so a client has something durable
  to condition its next write on. Nothing enforces a precondition yet; that is `P1-T7b` and `P1-T7c`.
  Focused tests, the full backend suite, and the full `web-app` suite pass.
- Tests added first:
  - `src/test/kotlin/.../migration/FieldValueSetRevisionContractTest.kt`, 4 Testcontainers
    PostgreSQL tests: a populated baseline where every set already stored gains its first revision
    while its answers and its own last-moved timestamp are left alone; a clean baseline where a new
    set defaults to its first revision and a set created below it is refused; a count that may move
    forward or stay put but is refused when asked to move backwards, leaving the stored count intact;
    and a repetition counting only its own changes rather than the root set's.
  - `src/test/kotlin/.../service/fields/FieldValueSetRevisionTest.kt`, 9 tests: one save with one
    change advancing by one; three changes in one save advancing once; a save that stores nothing
    leaving the count alone; two consecutive saves advancing one step at a time; a read carrying the
    tag of the current state; a save carrying the tag of the state it produced and not the one it
    replaced; a tag from one set never equalling a tag from another at the same count; a freshly
    assigned schema starting at the first revision; and a materialized configured default advancing
    the fresh set once.
  - `src/test/kotlin/.../resource/exchange/ExchangeFieldsResourceETagTest.kt`, 4 tests: the Fields
    read, the value save, and the schema assignment each carrying the tag the service resolved, and a
    projection with no set of answers carrying no tag rather than an invented one.
  - `src/test/kotlin/.../repository/fields/FieldValueRevisionPersistenceContractTest.kt` gained 2
    `@QuarkusTest` tests against a migrated PostgreSQL container: the count surviving the round trip
    through the mapped entity, and the database refusing to move a set back to an earlier state when
    the request arrives through Hibernate rather than through raw SQL. These were added to the
    existing class rather than a new one so the same container and seeded fixture are reused.
- Failure observed before implementation:
  - Migration: 4 run, 0 failures, 4 errors, all `column "revision" does not exist` or

- Decisions made:
  - One save is one change to the set, however many of its questions that save answered. The client
    posts every editable field on each save, so counting answers written would make the count a
    measure of form width rather than of edits, and two clients editing different fields of the same
    form would see the count jump by different amounts for the same action.
  - The count is carried by an ordinary column that the service increments, not by a JPA `@Version`.
    `@Version` would have given race safety for free, but it also takes ownership of the value away
    from the service, changes what `save` means for a set created with a non-zero initial value, and
    would have to be introduced without a test that demonstrates the race it fixes. The race is real
    and is recorded below as the exact thing `P1-T7b` must close, using the pessimistic
    `BaseRepository.findByIdForUpdate` the repository already uses to serialize competing writers.
  - Monotonicity is enforced by a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger rather than by convention, matching how
    `V80` enforces revision immutability. An update that leaves the count alone stays an ordinary
    update, so nothing that rewrites a set for another reason is blocked.
  - The `DEFAULT 1` is kept rather than dropped after the backfill, so an application version that
    predates the column can still create a set during a rolling deploy. This is weaker than the
    strict rule `V79` and `V80` take for their own columns, and deliberately so: an old writer that
    omits the count produces a correct first-state set, whereas an old writer that omits authorship
    produces a row whose author is unknowable.
  - The validator names the set as well as the count, so a tag taken from one set can never be spent
    against another. This costs nothing today, when an assignment has one root set, and is what keeps
    the tag safe once an assignment holds repetitions beside the answers it gives as itself.
  - The tag is carried on `SchemaAssignmentDto` rather than derived in the resource, because the
    resource is a thin adapter and deriving a validator is a decision about what identifies a state.
    Carrying it in the body as well as the header is deliberate: a client that cannot read response
    headers can still round-trip it.
  - The tag is derived only from the set's identity and count, so it does not change when the Schema
    Definition's display name is edited even though the projection carries that name. The tag
    validates the answers, which is what a conditional write is about; a renamed schema does not make
    a client's pending edit stale.
  - `materializeConfiguredDefaults` advances the fresh set to its second revision rather than being
    special-cased to leave it at the first. A default is a stored answer like any other, and the
    special case would buy nothing: the set is created and populated inside one transaction, so no
    client ever observes the first state of a set that has defaults.
  - The two new persistence tests were added to `FieldValueRevisionPersistenceContractTest` and its
    class documentation was widened, rather than creating a second `@QuarkusTest` class. A new class
    would start a second PostgreSQL container for a fixture the existing one already seeds.
- Assumptions: none new. The existing assumption that `field_contract` rows are never deleted is
  untouched by this subtask. Docker was available, so all six Testcontainers tests really ran.
- Industry-neutrality audit: `revision`, `ck_field_value_set_revision`,
  `field_value_set_revision_is_monotonic`, `trg_field_value_set_revision_monotonic`,
  `FieldValueSetETag`, `advanceValueSet`, `etag`, and `validated` all use platform vocabulary.
  Fixtures keep the neutral `process` namespace with the `recorded-note` and `recorded-options` keys,

  The capability was exercised against two materially different neutral patterns through the same

- Known risks or blockers: none blocking `P1-T7b`.
  - New and important: two concurrent saves can read the same count, both write the next one, and the
    trigger permits it because equal is not backwards. The result is two different answer states
    sharing one validator. Nothing enforces a precondition yet, so nothing is currently wrong for a
    client, but `P1-T7b` must not implement `If-Match` as a bare compare-and-set: it has to read the
    set through `BaseRepository.findByIdForUpdate` inside the mutation transaction so competing
    writers serialize, and it needs a test that two concurrent saves cannot both succeed.
  - New: the `@Version`-free count means Hibernate will not detect a lost update on the set by
    itself. This is the same gap as above and closes with the same change.
  - New: `FieldValueSetETag` derives but does not parse. Parsing an `If-Match` header, including a

  recipient, a registered application, and a service principal are all expressible and none of them

- Decisions made:
  - The legacy-consistency check is strict: a legacy App User key must be accompanied by the matching
    canonical `USER` pair. The consequence is that an application version older than `V80` can write
    neither a Field Value nor a Schema Assignment. This is the same rolling-deploy consequence `V79`
    already carries for Field Values and both files ship together, so the drain requirement is
    unchanged. A tolerant check was rejected because it readmits the exact state the backfill removed
    and would make a later drop of the legacy column lose authorship silently.
  - Existing Field Values are backfilled with one revision each rather than starting the series empty.
    A stored answer's `provenance`, `updated_at`, and author already assert "as of this moment, this
    principal left this value", so a revision built from exactly those columns invents nothing and
    makes every existing answer addressable from the upgrade forward. A value whose author was never
    recorded gets a revision that names no principal, which is why the revision's principal columns
    are nullable while every revision the application writes always fills them.
  - `revision_number` counts recorded changes within the Value Set and question, not versions of the
    row since creation. A backfilled revision is number 1 because it is the first change this system
    recorded, and the plain reading of the column is deliberately "the nth recorded change".
  - A revision holds `field_value_id`, `field_value_set_id`, and `schema_assignment_id` as plain
    identities with no foreign keys, because removing a Schema Assignment removes all three while the
    history must survive. `field_contract_id` is a real foreign key because a published contract
    version is never deleted, verified by grep over every deletion path in the Fields services.
  - Immutability is enforced by a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger rather than by convention, and `DELETE` is
    deliberately left permitted so the later retention and record-disposal work can act on a
    revision. The claim the trigger makes is exactly "a recorded revision is never rewritten".
  - A write whose stored state would be byte-identical, including the recording principal, session,
    and origin, stores nothing and records nothing. The Details form posts every editable field on
    each save, so counting those repeats as changes would fill the history with entries recording
    nothing having happened. The invariant this preserves is that the newest revision always says the
    same thing as the live answer. Numbers are compared with `compareTo` because the column pads
    every answer to its own scale.
  - `FieldValueProvenance` was left alone. It records how a value came to exist, and the new canonical
    columns record who; an application caller still writes `USER` provenance through the ordinary
    caller-supplied path rather than `API`, because changing that would reinterpret existing rows.
  - Chosen option codes go into a child table mirroring `field_value_selection` rather than a JSON
    column, matching the normalization direction the repository has already taken.
  - No `updated_at` was added to `schema_assignment`. Nothing mutates an assignment today, so the
    column would have no writer beyond creation. "Update timestamps" is satisfied by `field_value`
    keeping its own and by `field_value_set.updated_at` now advancing with its youngest answer, which
    is also the persisted value `P1-T7` derives its ETag from.
  - The non-secret session reference is real rather than reserved. `EndpointVerificationFilter`
    already resolves and validates the `UserSession` row for every authenticated request, so exposing
    it on `AuthTokenContext` and `AuthorizationContext` gives the column a writer today instead of
    leaving a column no path fills. No authentication decision was touched.
  - The Fields audit payload carries counts, the resource, the schema version, and the acting
    principal kind, never a value. `AuditEventDraftValidator` already prohibits `fieldValue` and
    `fieldValues` keys, and the audit test asserts the draft validates and that no answer text
    appears in any payload.
- Assumptions: `field_contract` rows are never deleted, verified by grep over every `delete` and

### 2026-08-31: `P1-T5` implemented

- Current phase and task: Phase 1. `P1-T5` complete; next task is `P1-T6`. The reusable
  value-foundation milestone (`P1-T5` through `P1-T9`) is now in progress.
- Status at session end: A typed answer belongs to a named set of answers rather than directly to
  the Schema Assignment. Every assignment that exists gained the one root set it answers with, every
  stored answer was carried into it, and value uniqueness moved from the assignment to the set, so
  one assignment can hold the same question once per repetition of a group. Existing Exchange reads,
  writes, and workflow conditions all address the root set only, so their behavior is unchanged.
  Focused tests and the full backend suite pass.

    second-root refusal, the two-answers-in-one-set refusal, the accepted same-question-per-set case,
    the cross-assignment set refusal and the pathless-repetition refusal, and an answer that names no

  - `SchemaAssignmentService` creates the root set with the assignment, materializes configured
    defaults into it, upserts every answer within it, projects `resolveValues` from it, and removes
    an assignment's sets after its answers. A write that finds no root set restores one, so an
    assignment created by a path that predates the set model can still be answered.
  - `ExchangeFieldQueryService` reads the root set, so a workflow condition about the Exchange never

  `usingBlueprintsArticle.tsx`. Read `usingExchangeFieldsArticle.tsx` in full and checked the matched
  statements in the others; every one is still accurate, including "Each Exchange has one primary
  schema assignment". No article, section, or registry size changed.
- Decisions made:
  - The Value Set can express a repetition from the start. A table that could only hold one set per
    assignment would make the uniqueness change a rename, since `(set, contract)` and
    `(assignment, contract)` would say the same thing forever. `set_kind` and `occurrence_path` are
    what make the new key mean something, and the migration test proves the same question can be
    answered once per set.
  - `parent_value_set_id` was deliberately not added. Nesting a repetition inside a repetition is
    designed in `P5-T2` together with the path grammar, and a nullable self-reference is a cheap
    later addition to a table holding only root rows.
  - Both stages of the expand-contract run in one migration, matching `V77`. The consequence is
    stated plainly under the compatibility rules and is covered by its own test: after `V79` an
    application version that predates it cannot insert a Field Value, because the column is
    `NOT NULL` and the old writer omits it. The service runs one task with
    `MinimumHealthyPercent: 100` and migrates at start, so a Field-value save issued by the old task
    during the changeover is refused. The alternative, a nullable column plus a contract stage in a
    later release, was rejected because it needs a heal path for answers written with no set and
    leaves an obligation no task owns until Phase 5.
  - A read tolerates a missing root set and projects no stored answers; a write restores it. The FK
    means an answer cannot reference a set that does not exist, so a missing root set really does
    mean the assignment holds no answers of its own, and a read that threw would take out the
    Details tab for a case a write can simply fix.
  - `unassignSchema` still removes answers by assignment rather than by set, because removing the
    assignment must remove every answer under it, repetitions included.
  - The root set is created in `assignSchema` rather than derived on demand, so the one-root rule is
    established by the same transaction that creates the assignment.
- Assumptions: `field_value` has no reader outside the Fields services and repositories, verified by
  grep over the Kotlin sources and every migration; the only remaining assignment-scoped value read
  is the deletion sweep in `unassignSchema`, and `FieldValueRepository.findByResource` has no
  production caller. Docker was available, so all six Testcontainers tests really ran.

    submitted offset, or null offset when the input carried none, and format back at that offset with

    canonical text. `NumberTypeContract` now refuses a number the column would reshape, and measures
    a configured scale against significant digits rather than raw ones, so `1.500` is accepted at
    scale 2 instead of refused.

- Decisions made:
  - A date-time is stored as the instant plus the submitted offset in a separate column, not as an
    `OffsetDateTime`. Reading an `OffsetDateTime` back from PostgreSQL yields the session offset, not
    the submitted one, so the offset has to be its own column for the answer to be reproducible.
  - An input carrying no offset is read as UTC and records no offset. That is the only deterministic
    reading available, and it makes a new no-offset input and a legacy row behave identically instead
    of inventing an offset for either. The client now always sends one.
  - The entity maps the `timestamptz` column to `java.sql.Timestamp`, matching how every other
    `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE` column in this codebase is mapped, rather than introducing the first
    `Instant`-mapped property. `Timestamp` is instant-correct across the driver, and
    `CanonicalFieldValue` still exposes an `Instant` so no caller handles a zone.
  - Numbers cross the API as digits in a JSON string rather than as JSON numbers. A
    `NUMERIC(38,10)` value cannot survive a client that parses JSON numbers as doubles, and the type
    contract already accepted string input, so the wire form is now symmetric. This is a read-shape
    change for any consumer doing arithmetic on the raw value; the first-party frontend was migrated
    in the same task.
  - The canonical text of a decimal is written at its contract's configured scale, which requires
    passing that scale into the codec. Without it the column's ten padding zeros reach the response
    and an integer answer of 5 reads as `5.0000000000`. A stored value that cannot be written at the
    configured scale without rounding is left at its own width rather than silently rounded.
  - A number wider than the column is refused with a validation message rather than left to the
    database. Previously an over-wide value was either rounded silently or produced a numeric
    overflow, so a responder could be told an answer was accepted and get a different one back.
  - The Boolean fix is client-side only. The backend, the codec, and the column already
    distinguished absent from No; only `toCanonicalValue`, the two-state switch, and the blueprint
    default builder collapsed the three readings. The backend tests for this are labelled regression
    tests above rather than presented as red.
  - `FieldValueEditor` was split rather than grown past the 150-line rule. The select controls moved
    to `FieldSelectEditor` and the Yes or No control to `FieldBooleanEditor`, leaving the dispatcher
    and the scalar controls.
  - The workflow applicability literal editor was fixed in the same task. It writes the literals the
    evaluator compares, so leaving it would have shipped an authoring UI that produces a wall-clock
    literal and a narrowed number against a backend that now reads moments and digits.
  - `V78` was changed from `SMALLINT` to `INTEGER` after `FieldValueMomentPersistenceContractTest`
    surfaced a Hibernate schema-validation failure. The file had only ever run in throwaway test
    containers, so it was not an applied migration.
- Assumptions: `field_value.datetime_value` has no other reader in SQL or code, verified by grep over
  every migration and the Kotlin sources. Docker was available, so both PostgreSQL contract tests and
  the Quarkus persistence test really ran.

- Decisions made:
  - The invariant key is a denormalised `field_definition_id` on the binding rather than a trigger.
    A unique index cannot span tables, and a plain column plus a composite foreign key keeps both
    the invariant and its consistency rule declarative.
  - Conflict resolution keeps the binding already carrying the most values, then the newest
    contract, then the earliest display position, then the lowest id. Favouring entered data first
    means the surviving binding is the one a customer is most likely to be using.
  - Every member of a conflicted group is preserved in `schema_field_binding_conflict`, including
    the retained one, so an operator can reconstruct what the version held. A migration notice would
    have been lost. The table has no JPA entity because no application code reads it; it is an
    operator-facing migration record, not a modelled domain table.
  - A value entered against a removed binding keeps its row, its text, and its contract. Only the
    pointer to the binding that no longer exists is cleared. The value is consequently no longer
    projected for that version, because the projection is binding-driven; that is the honest result
    of resolving an ambiguous configuration and it is recorded in the conflict table.
  - The migration resolves rather than fails. Refusing to upgrade would strand an operator with no
    way to correct an immutable published version.
  - `ux_binding_contract` is kept. It is implied by the new index given the consistency foreign key,
    but it states a distinct rule cheaply and contracting it is not this task's job.
  - `mapBindings` still derives the stable field from the contract rather than from the new column.
    The composite foreign key guarantees the two agree, and leaving the read path alone kept the
    change to the writers.

- Decisions made:
  - A Schema Assignment change requires `Capability.EXCHANGE_ADMIN` through a new dedicated Action
    rather than reusing `EXCHANGE_SHARE` or the write capability. Only the `OWNER` share role holds
    it, and the initiator's `OWNER` share is granted before `applyCreationTimeFields` runs, so
    creation-time assignment is unaffected.
  - `authorizeManageSchema` has no default implementation. A default delegating to the value-write
    rule would silently give a future adapter the weaker check.
  - A write to a binding outside the caller's audience reuses the "not part of the assigned schema"
    message. Confirming that such a binding exists would leak the very fact the audience filter
    hides.
  - Binding defaults are materialised as stored values at assignment rather than projected lazily on
    read, so `ExchangeFieldQueryService` and Workflow conditions observe the same value the
    projection shows, and there is one source of truth.
  - An uncanonicalisable configured default is skipped with a warning. Failing the assignment would
    leave a resource with no way forward, since the published version cannot be corrected in place.
  - Authoring-time validation of `defaultValueJson` in `SchemaDefinitionService.persistBindings` was
    deliberately not added in this task. The settings UI has no producer for that field today, so
    the gap is not reachable from the product; it should be closed alongside the wider Schema
    authoring work.
  - `AuditMigrationUpgradeContractTest` no longer pins the head to a literal `"75"`. It now reads
    the highest migration on disk, which keeps the contract about the full chain applying cleanly
    instead of requiring an edit from every future migration.
